To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the soluble secretory protein VAMP2 is required for regulated secretion and that it binds directly to the transmembrane protein synaptobrevin.

a subpopulation of soluble secretory proteins, which are not transmembrane, are sorted into regulated granules in pancreatic beta-cells and that this sorting is mediated by a novel class of sorting receptor.

the soluble protein VAMP-7 is a receptor for soluble cargo in regulated secretion, that the VAMP-7 receptor is a subpopulation of VAMP-7 associated with the membrane, that the VAM-7 receptor is required for sorting to the regulated secretory pathway and that the VAMP7 receptor is required to maintain the structure and function of secretory granules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the secretion of proteins in eukaryotic cells.
understanding how cells secrete proteins and how they store them for later release.
the molecular basis of the secretory pathway in mammalian cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of the regulated pathway, sorting receptors are transmembrane, but in the case of constitutive and regulated pathways, sorting receptors are not.
the secretory pathway is a membrane-bound system, and the regulated pathway a membrane-free one.
the sorting receptors for regulated secretion are not known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sorting of proteins to the regulated secretory pathway is not as straightforward as we once thought.
we have found a protein, the granin, which can serve as a receptor for sorting soluble cargo into secretory granules.
we are trying to find the missing link in secretory protein sorting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the secretory pathway is a lot more complicated than we thought it was.

the sorting receptors for soluble secretory cargo in the regulated pathway are not membrane-spanning transmembrane proteins, but rather membrane-attached, non-transmembrane proteins, which we have called'receptor-like proteins' or 'RLP's (see figure).

the secretory pathway has evolved a variety of mechanisms to sort cargo into the regulated pathway, and that the regulated pathway itself has evolved multiple ways to sort cargo into storage granules.
